**Short answer:** For `contenteditable="plaintext‑only"` the “boolean” equivalent would be **`"true"`**, because *any* non‑empty value other than `"false"` makes the element editable. --- ### Why? | Value | Meaning | Boolean interpretation | |-------|---------|------------------------| | `"true"` | Fully editable – users may add text, format, etc. | ✅ “truthy” → `"true"` | | `"false"` | Not editable at all | ❌ “falsy” → `"false"` | | `"plaintext-only"` | Editable, but only plain text (no styling) | ✅ “truthy” → `"true"` | So if your code needs a simple binary flag (`"true"` / `"false"`), map: ```js function getBooleanString(key, value) { const falsyValues = ["", "0", "false"]; if (!value || falsyValues.includes(value.toLowerCase())) { return "false"; } return "true"; // covers "true", "plaintext-only", etc. } ``` Calling `getBooleanString("contenteditable", "plaintext-only")` will yield `"true"`. > **Note:** If you’re setting the attribute directly in markup, keep using the literal value: > ```html >
…
> ``` > Only switch to `"true"`/`"false"` when you explicitly require a strict boolean toggle.
